entries.h: Every setup answers the same five questions
entries.t:
The common thread
Every setup answers the same five questions
The pairs and timeframes change. The sequence does not. If one answer is missing, there is no trade.
01 · LOCATION
Is price at a higher-timeframe zone?
A fresh 4H or 1H supply or demand zone that caused a break of structure. This sets direction.
02 · LIQUIDITY
Whose stops were just taken?
Price should run a prior low (for longs) or high (for shorts) as it enters the zone. That is the fuel.
03 · CONFIRMATION
Did lower-timeframe structure shift?
A displacement candle closes through the last opposing swing: the market structure shift (MSS).
04 · ENTRY
Where is the refined zone?
The order block that produced the shift, ideally with an imbalance sitting on top of it.
05 · TARGET
Where is price drawn to?
The nearest opposing zone or pool of liquidity. It must pay at least 1:2 from the stop.
ALWAYS
What proves me wrong?
The swing that launched the shift. The stop goes beyond it and risk is fixed before the order is placed.

entries.h: HTF zone → LTF shift → order block
entries.t:
The model
HTF zone → LTF shift → order block
| Stage | Timeframe | What you need to see (long) | For shorts
| 1. Location | 4H (or 1H) | The 4H has swept a low and shifted bullish. Price has pulled back into the discount half of the leg, either into a fresh demand zone (USD/JPY) or to internal lows left inside the leg. | 4H swept a high and shifted bearish. Pullback into premium: fresh supply, or internal highs (XAU/USD).
| 2. Liquidity | 30m | A low of the pullback is taken while price is at that location. | A high is taken. Expect more than one sweep.
| 3. Confirmation | 30m | A displacement candle closes above the last lower high (MSS). | Close below the last higher low (15m in the XAU/USD case).
| 4. Entry | 15m | Unmitigated order block at the origin of the displacement, with an imbalance beside it. Buy limit at its top edge. | Sell limit at the OB's bottom edge.
| 5. Stop | 15m | Below the protected low that launched the MSS, plus a buffer. Tighter variant: just below the order block. | Above the protected high, plus buffer and spread. Tighter variant: just above the order block.
| 6. Target | 30m | Near edge of the first opposing supply zone, or just before a pool of untouched buy-side liquidity (GBP/JPY). Minimum 1:2. | Near edge of the first opposing demand.
USD/JPY used a 4H / 30m / 15m ladder and XAU/USD used 4H / 1H / 15m with the shift read on the 15m. The same logic can be stepped down (1H / 15m / 5m) as long as the three roles stay separate: one chart for location, one for confirmation, one for entry.

Constant in all eleven
A liquidity sweep comes first, then a lower-timeframe shift, then a limit order at the near edge of the order block usually with an imbalance beside it. Six fills only just reached that edge. The first Bitcoin, AUD/USD and second USD/JPY fills went deep, and the second GBP/JPY trade dipped halfway into the block after filling, so the stop has to sit beyond the structure, not inside the block.
The target varies
It is whatever stands first in the way: an opposing zone, or a pool of untouched liquidity. With a liquidity target, exit a few pips before the level.
Liquidity in front of the entry
In both GBP/JPY trades, AUD/USD, GBP/AUD, the second USD/JPY and both BTC/USD trades, lows sitting above the zone were swept before the fill, after waits of under two hours to a day. A bounce above an untouched zone is not the entry. See Inducement. If stops rest between price and your OB, expect them to be taken first.
All eleven are confirmation entries. The order is always sweep, shift, zone; the second Bitcoin case spells that out. See Entry models for how that differs from an aggressive entry at the zone.
Eleven winning examples from one author are a description of a style, not evidence that it is profitable. The table is here so you know what to look for when you backtest.

entries.h: What to do, in order
entries.t:
Daily routine
What to do, in order
Before the session
Mark 4H structure on each pair you trade.Last break of structure, the current swing high and low, and the 50% level of that leg.
Mark the fresh zones and the internal liquidity.Demand in discount, supply in premium. Also mark internal highs and lows left inside the last 4H leg. Delete any zone that has already been tapped.
Set alerts at the near edge of each zone and at each internal high or low.Then close the chart. Pairs sitting in the middle of their range are not candidates today.
Check the news calendar.Note high-impact releases for the currencies involved. Do not leave a limit order resting through one.
When an alert fires
Map the 30m delivery into the zone.Lower highs, lower lows, the last low, and the opposing zone at the origin of the move.
Wait for the sweep and the MSS.A low is taken, price fails to continue, and a candle closes above the last lower high with displacement.
Refine on the 15m.Find the order block and imbalance left by the displacement. Mark the protected low, which is often a final sweep just before the shift.
Measure before you place.Entry, stop, target. If it does not pay 1:2 to the first opposing zone, skip it.
Place entry, stop and target as one order.Size for fixed risk. Write down the reason in one sentence.
After the trade
Screenshot all three timeframes.Before and after. Do it for losers and for setups you skipped as well.
Log it.See the journal fields below. Review the log weekly, not trade by trade.

entries.h: Where the stop and the target go
entries.t:
Order rules
Where the stop and the target go
Entry
Limit order at the near edge of the order block.
Placed when the MSS candle closes.
Near edge fills more often than the midpoint. Use the midpoint only if the OB is unusually tall.
Buys fill on the ask: add the spread to a buy limit.
Cancel if price covers about half the distance to target without a fill.
Stop loss
Beyond the swing that launched the MSS.
Long: below the protected low. Short: above the protected high.
The swing is the real invalidation. The XAU/USD chart used a tighter stop just beyond the order block: more reward per unit of risk, and more often stopped by a deep wick. Pick one placement and test it.
Add a buffer of a few pips. On shorts add the spread too, because buy stops trigger on the ask.
Never widen a stop after entry. Never size the stop to fit a lot size; size the lot to fit the stop.
Take profit
Near edge of the first opposing zone.
Usually the supply or demand at the origin of the move that delivered price into your HTF zone.
Liquidity along the way (trendline highs, equal highs) supports the target. It does not replace it.
Set it a few pips short of the zone edge.
If no zone stands in the way, target untouched liquidity (old highs or lows) and exit a few pips before it.
Under 1:2, there is no trade.

entries.h: The rules that keep you in the game
entries.t:
Risk
The rules that keep you in the game
Per trade and per day
Risk a fixed 0.5–1% of the account on every trade. Same risk on the setup you love and the one you doubt.
Stop for the day after two losses.
Do not hold two trades that are the same bet, such as longs on USD/JPY and EUR/JPY together, at full risk each.
What the win rate has to be
Break-even win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + reward-to-risk), before costs.
| Reward : risk | Break-even win rate
| 1:2 | 33.3%
| 1:3 | 25%
| 1:4 | 20%
At 1:3 you can lose most of your trades and still make money, but only if every loss is exactly 1R. Losing streaks of five or more are normal at these win rates.
On profitability
No pattern guarantees profit. An edge shows up only across many trades taken the same way. Backtest this model on at least 50 occurrences, record the real win rate and average R, then trade it small on live data before sizing up.

entries.h: Labels used on the charts
entries.t:
Glossary
Labels used on the charts
| Label | Meaning as used here
| HTF / LTF | Higher timeframe (direction and location) and lower timeframe (confirmation and entry).
| BoS | Break of structure. Price breaks a swing in the direction of the current trend. On the 30m chart it marks the final low broken on the way into demand.
| MSS | Market structure shift. Price closes through the last swing against the current trend, for example above the last lower high in a downtrend. The first sign of reversal.
| CHoCH | Change of character. The first break against the current internal trend. Used on the entry models slides for the same event the other posts label MSS.
| Displacement | A fast, large-bodied move that leaves an imbalance. Shows intent behind a break.
| IDM | Inducement. The first pullback low (or high) after a structure shift. Early traders enter there and their stops become liquidity for the real pullback. See Inducement.
| IMB | Imbalance, also called a fair value gap. A range price moved through too quickly for both sides to trade. Price often returns to it.
| OB | Order block. The last opposing candle before a displacement move. Used as the refined entry zone.
| Supply / demand | Zones where a strong move down or up began. Fresh means price has not returned since.
| $$$ | Liquidity. Stops and breakout orders resting above highs (buy-side) or below lows (sell-side), often along a trendline.
| X | Marks a liquidity sweep: the spot where a wick ran a high or low and price reversed.
| BSL / SSL | Buy-side liquidity (stops above highs) and sell-side liquidity (stops below lows).
| EQL / EQH | Equal lows / equal highs. Two or more swings at the same price, with a thick layer of stops beyond them.
| Sweep | Price trades through a high or low to trigger the orders there, then reverses.
| Premium / discount | Upper and lower half of a price leg. Sell in premium, buy in discount.
| Protected low / high | The swing that launched a break of structure. If it is taken, the break has failed.
| R | One unit of risk: the distance from entry to stop. A 1:3 trade pays 3R.

entries.p: Good vs Bad Break of Structure
entries.h: Introduction
entries.t:
Concept
Good vs bad break of structure
Two uptrends can print the same break of structure and leave very different lows behind. If the pullback swept the previous low before price broke higher, the new low is protected. If it did not, the lows underneath are still untouched, and price is likely to come back for them. The second kind is where zone entries get stopped out.

entries.p: Good vs Bad Break of Structure
entries.h: Good BoS: the pullback sweeps the last low first
entries.t:
Chart: Line drawing of an uptrend. Price makes a high, pulls back to a low, breaks the high, then pulls back below the previous low, marked X, before rallying to break the latest high. An arrow points to the sweep low.
Slide 1 — “Good BoS: Swept liquidity before creating a new higher high, leaving a protected low.”
1 · The idea
Good BoS: the pullback sweeps the last low first
What the drawing shows
A normal uptrend. A high, a pullback low, then a break above the high (the first BoS).
A deeper second pullback. It goes under the previous pullback low. That is the X.
The break. From that sweep low price rallies and breaks the latest high (the second BoS).
Why the new low is protected
Buyers from the first leg had stops under the first pullback low. The sweep took them. There is no clean low left under the new one, so price has less reason to come back down. The new low also launched a break of structure, which makes it the level the uptrend now depends on.
A sweep, not a close
A line drawing cannot show wicks. In the candle example below, price dips under the earlier low and turns straight back up. If price closes below the previous low and stays there, that is structure breaking down, not a sweep.

entries.p: Good vs Bad Break of Structure
entries.h: Bad BoS: a higher low with stops still under it
entries.t:
Chart: Line drawing of an uptrend. Price makes a high, pulls back to a low, breaks the high, pulls back to a higher low without reaching the previous low, and breaks the latest high. An arrow points to the higher low.
Slide 2 — “Bad BoS: Did not sweep liquidity before breaking structure. This leaves an unprotected low with high potential to be swept in the future.”
2 · The contrast
Bad BoS: a higher low with stops still under it
What the drawing shows
The same uptrend. High, pullback low, break.
A shallow second pullback. It stops above the previous low. A tidy higher low.
The break. Price breaks the latest high all the same.
Why the low is unprotected
Nothing was taken. Stops are still under the first low, and new stops are now under the second. That is two layers of sell-side liquidity stacked under price. The post says such a low has “high potential to be swept in the future”.
“Bad” does not mean the break is fake. Price did make a higher high. It means the low is a poor place to buy from and a poor place to hide a stop behind.
Rule to carry forward
After every break of structure, look at the low it came from and ask one question: did that low take out the low before it? If yes, it is protected. If no, mark it as liquidity.

entries.p: Good vs Bad Break of Structure
entries.h: Example: the good break holds
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Two breaks of structure upward. Before the second, price dips under an earlier low, marked X, and a large bullish candle follows. A demand zone is drawn from that sweep low. Price rallies to a high marked BSL, returns into the zone, and the long from the top of the zone reaches the BSL.
Slide 3 — “Example, Good BoS. Swept liquidity before creating a new higher high, leaving a protected low.”
3 · On a chart
Example: the good break holds
What happened
An uptrend with a BoS. Then a pullback.
The sweep (X). The pullback dips under an earlier low. A large bullish candle follows at once.
The second BoS. Price breaks the previous high and keeps climbing to a new one. That high is marked BSL.
The zone. A box from the sweep low up to the base of the rally.
The return. Price falls back and dips into the upper part of the zone.
The result. It turns there and rallies through the BSL.
The position box
Entry at the top edge of the zone.
Stop at the bottom of the zone, which is the sweep low.
Target at the BSL, about 2.6 times the stop.
The pullback into the zone never came near the sweep low. There was nothing left under it to take.

entries.p: Good vs Bad Break of Structure
entries.h: Example: the bad break fails
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Two breaks of structure upward. An order block is drawn at a pullback low that sits above an earlier, untouched low marked with a line. Price rallies to a high marked BSL, returns to the order block, bounces about halfway to the target, then falls through the order block, the earlier low and the stop.
Slide 4 — “Example, Bad BoS. Did not sweep liquidity before breaking structure. Leaves an unprotected low.”
4 · On a chart
Example: the bad break fails
What happened
An uptrend with a BoS. A pullback leaves a low. The line under the chart is drawn from it.
A higher low. The next pullback stops above that line. The order block (OB) is drawn here.
The second BoS. Price breaks higher and runs to a new high, marked BSL.
The return. Price falls back and taps the top of the order block. The long fills.
A bounce. Price climbs roughly halfway to the target.
The failure. It rolls over, goes through the order block, through the earlier low and through the stop. The last wick ends well below.
The position box
Entry at the top edge of the order block.
Stop under the order block. As far as I can read the slide, it sits just beneath the earlier low.
Target at the BSL, about 3 times the stop. Not reached. The trade lost 1R.
On the way up, this chart looked the same as the good one: two breaks, a zone, a return to the zone. The difference was underneath. An untouched low sat just below the order block, and price went and took it.
The bounce is the dangerous part
The trade was in profit by roughly 1.4R, measured from the box, before it failed. A trader who moved the stop to break-even there lost nothing. A trader who held for the full target lost 1R. Neither changes the lesson: the entry was at a zone with liquidity under it.

entries.p: Good vs Bad Break of Structure
entries.h: Protected or unprotected?
entries.t:
Telling them apart
Protected or unprotected?
Chart: Cover slide: Good vs Bad Break of Structure. Two line drawings side by side. On the left the second pullback sweeps the previous low, marked X. On the right the second pullback makes a higher low.
Cover — good on the left, bad on the right.
The check has to be made before the order is placed. The first row comes from the slides. The others are my additions, drawn from the case studies.
| Check | Protected low (good BoS) | Unprotected low (bad BoS)
| Did the low take out the low before it? | Yes. There is an X | No. It is a higher low
| What is under the zone? | Only the sweep low itself | One or more clean, untouched lows
| How did price leave the low? | Fast, usually one large candle with an imbalance | Often a steady climb
| Is it at a higher-timeframe zone? | Often. The sweep runs into HTF demand | Often mid-leg, above any HTF zone
| What to do | Buy the zone at the low | Mark the low as liquidity. Wait for it to be swept, or pass
A bad BoS can become a good setup
In the losing example, price ended by sweeping the unprotected low. That sweep is step one of the sequence on this site. If price then shifts structure back up with an imbalance, the zone that shift leaves is the one to buy. The slide does not show what happened next, so this is a rule to test, not a result.
Not a guarantee in either direction
Protected lows are broken when the trend ends. Unprotected lows sometimes hold for a long time in a strong trend, and waiting for the sweep means missing those moves. The post says “high potential”, not certainty.

entries.h: Entry, stop loss and take profit
entries.t:
Order placement
Entry, stop loss and take profit
For the long after a good break, as drawn on slide 3.
Entry
Buy limit at the top edge of the zone at the protected low.
The zone runs from the sweep low up to the base of the candle that launched the break.
The example filled in the upper part of the zone.
Only place the order once the break of structure has closed.
Stop loss
Below the sweep low, plus a buffer.
The grey box on slide 3 ends at the sweep low. Go a little beyond the wick.
If that low breaks, the protected low has failed and the uptrend is in question.
If an untouched low sits under your stop, the stop is not safe. That is the losing example.
Take profit
The BSL: the high made after the break.
About 2.6R in the example.
Set the order a little before the line.
Skip the trade if the high is closer than twice the stop.

entries.h: Step-by-step for the next trade
entries.t:
Repeatable strategy
Step-by-step for the next trade
Written for longs. For shorts, mirror it: a good break down comes after a high is swept.
Find the last break of structure in the trend direction.Mark the low it launched from.
Did that low sweep the low before it?Yes: protected. Go to step 4. No: unprotected. Go to step 3.
Unprotected: mark it as liquidity and do not buy the zone.Set an alert under the low. If it is swept and price shifts back up, treat that as a new setup.
Protected: draw the zone from the sweep low to the base of the launch candle.Check that nothing clean and untouched lies beneath it.
Mark the high made after the break.That is the BSL and the target.
Buy limit at the top edge of the zone, stop below the sweep low.At least 1:2 to the target.
Size, place, hold, record.Risk 0.5–1%. Note in the journal whether the low was protected.

Where this has already appeared
Every case study on this site took its entry from a low or high that followed a sweep. The comparison table in the playbook has a row for it, “Sweep before the LTF shift”, and it reads yes in all eleven.

entries.h: Introduction
entries.t:
Entry models
Aggressive entry and confirmation entry
Two ways to get into the same idea. Both sell a pullback into supply after structure has turned bearish. The difference is how much proof you ask for before the order goes in, and what that proof costs you.
Both drawn as shorts
Schematics, not live charts
Mirror for longs
From the post
“Aggressive Entry: Taking positions early based on established market context and protected swing points without waiting for minor structural confirmations. Confirmation Entry: Waiting for a clear internal shift, a change of character (CHoCH), or a mitigation of premium and discount zones before executing. No guesswork. Just pure rules, patience, and structure.”
1 · Aggressive entry
2 · Confirmation entry
Side by side
Which one to use
In the case studies
How to read this page
These two slides are line drawings of idealised price, so every swing is clean. Real charts are messier. X marks a liquidity sweep. $$$ marks resting liquidity along a trendline. EQH is equal highs. CHoCH (change of character) is the first break against the current internal trend; the earlier posts label the same event MSS. Reward-to-risk figures are measured from the drawn boxes and are illustrative only.

entries.h: Aggressive entry (with context)
entries.t:
Chart: Line diagram of the aggressive entry. Price rallies, sweeps a prior high to form the protected high, drops through a previous low leaving an imbalance, breaks structure again, forms equal highs, then returns into the supply zone under the protected high, where the short is entered. The target is the last low.
Model 1 — “Aggressive Entry (with context).”
Model 1
Aggressive entry (with context)
You sell the zone when price touches it. There is no lower-timeframe signal first. What makes that reasonable is the context built up before price returns.
Reading the drawing, left to right
A rally with a trendline of lows ($$$). Price makes higher highs (the first BoS) and its lows line up on a dotted trendline. Stops from buyers collect beneath that line.
The final high sweeps the previous one (X). Price pokes above the prior high, takes the buy-side liquidity there and turns. This high becomes the protected high.
A drop breaks structure. Price falls through the trendline and through the low the rally began from (the lower BoS line). The move is fast enough to leave an imbalance (IMB).
Supply is drawn at the origin. The zone runs from the protected high down to where the drop began, with the imbalance directly beneath it.
Structure breaks down again. Price bounces, then makes another lower low (the second lower BoS). The downtrend is now established, not a one-off.
Equal highs form under the zone (EQH). The bounces stall at the same price twice. Sellers put stops above that double top, right in front of supply.
Price returns. It runs the equal highs, fills the imbalance and enters the supply zone. The short is entered at the zone's bottom edge.
Price falls to the last low. The target line is drawn across it.
The context that justifies entering without confirmation
The zone's high swept liquidity before the drop.
The move away from the zone broke structure and left an imbalance.
Structure has broken in the same direction a second time.
The zone is fresh. This is the first return.
Liquidity (equal highs) sits in front of the zone, so price has a reason to reach it, and those stops are taken as you are filled.
Orders
Entry: sell limit at the bottom edge of supply.
Stop loss: just above the protected high. On the drawing the grey box ends a fraction above the line.
Take profit: the most recent low. On the drawing this is about 3.8 times the risk.
The target line is labelled “BSL” on this slide. It sits under a low, which is sell-side liquidity, and the second slide labels the equivalent level “SSL”. I am treating the label as a slip.

entries.h: Confirmation entry
entries.t:
Chart: Line diagram of the confirmation entry. Price drops from a supply zone, climbs back in a staircase along a trendline, sweeps a high as it taps the supply zone, then breaks the last higher low (CHoCH). A smaller supply zone forms under the new protected high, and the short is entered on the pullback into it. The target is the sell-side liquidity at the low.
Model 2 — “Confirmation Entry.”
Model 2
Confirmation entry
Price reaches the zone and you do nothing yet. You wait for the internal structure of the pullback to break, then sell the first retracement after that break.
Reading the drawing, left to right
A drop from supply breaks structure. The large supply zone at the top is the origin of the fall through the BoS line. The low of that fall is marked SSL: sell-side liquidity, and the eventual target.
The pullback climbs in a staircase. Higher highs and higher lows, each previous high broken (the short dotted lines). Internally, the trend is up.
Its lows sit on a trendline ($$$). More sell-side liquidity building under the pullback.
Price taps the supply zone and sweeps a high (X). The last push takes the previous internal high and reaches into the zone. The zone has now been mitigated. The aggressive trader is already short from the zone's edge.
CHoCH. Price turns and breaks below the most recent higher low. This is the first time the staircase has failed. The drop leaves an imbalance.
A new, smaller supply forms. It runs from the high made inside the big zone, now the protected high, down to the start of the CHoCH move.
Price retraces into the small supply. The short is entered at its bottom edge.
Price falls to the SSL. Through the trendline lows on the way.
What the confirmation adds
Proof that the higher-timeframe zone is being defended. If price had gone straight through it, no CHoCH would have printed and there would be no trade.
A protected high that formed at the zone, giving a precise invalidation.
A second, refined zone to enter from.
Orders
Entry: sell limit at the bottom edge of the small supply left by the CHoCH.
Stop loss: above the protected high. On the drawing the grey box ends on the line, so add a buffer and the spread.
Take profit: the SSL, the low that the pullback started from. On the drawing this is about 2.9 times the risk.
The cost
The entry is lower than the aggressive trader's and comes later. And if price drops away after the CHoCH without retracing, there is no fill at all.

entries.h: Same idea, different amounts of proof
entries.t:
Side by side
Same idea, different amounts of proof
| | Aggressive entry | Confirmation entry
| What you need before price arrives | A zone whose high swept liquidity and whose drop broke structure and left an imbalance. Trend confirmed by a further break. | A zone that caused a break of structure. Less is required up front.
| What you need when price arrives | Nothing. The limit order is already resting. | A tap of the zone, a sweep of an internal high, then a CHoCH with an imbalance.
| Entry | Near edge of the original zone | Near edge of the smaller zone left by the CHoCH
| Stop loss | Beyond the protected high at the top of the zone | Beyond the protected high formed during the tap
| Take profit | The last low | The last low (SSL)
| On the drawings | ≈ 1:3.8 | ≈ 1:2.9
| When the zone fails | You are in the trade and take the full loss. | No CHoCH prints, so you are usually not in the trade.
| When the zone holds | You are always filled. | You are filled only if price retraces after the CHoCH.
| Screen time | Low. Set the order and an alert. | Higher. Someone has to see the CHoCH and place the order.
The two reward-to-risk numbers come from different drawings with different scales, so they show the direction of the trade-off and not its size.
How the two fit together
Look at the confirmation drawing from the CHoCH onward: a high that swept liquidity, a break of structure with an imbalance, a fresh zone, and a limit order at its edge. That is the aggressive model again, one level down. This is my observation, not a claim made in the post, and it explains why the two never conflict. Confirmation means waiting for the aggressive setup to appear on a smaller scale inside the larger zone.

entries.h: Choosing between them
entries.t:
Which one to use
Choosing between them
The post defines the two models and does not say when to prefer one. The guidance below is mine.
Lean aggressive when
The trade is with the higher-timeframe trend.
The zone is fresh, was born from a sweep and broke structure with an imbalance.
Liquidity sits in front of the zone (equal highs or lows, or a trendline).
The zone is narrow enough that a stop beyond it still pays at least 1:2.
You cannot watch the chart when price is likely to arrive.
Lean confirmation when
The trade is against the higher-timeframe trend, or the trend is unclear.
The zone is wide, so a stop beyond it is too large.
The zone is old or has been touched before.
Price is arriving fast, with large candles and no hesitation.
Nothing has been swept on the way into the zone.
Checklist: aggressive entry (short)
Did the high sweep a prior high before turning?Mark it as the protected high.
Did the drop from it break a swing low and leave an imbalance?Draw supply from the protected high down to the start of the drop.
Has structure broken down again since?A second lower low shows the trend is in place.
Is the zone untouched, with liquidity resting below it?Equal highs under the zone are ideal.
Does it pay at least 1:2 to the last low?Sell limit at the bottom edge, stop above the protected high, target the low. Place all three together.
Checklist: confirmation entry (short)
Is price inside a supply zone that caused a break of structure?Set the alert at its bottom edge and wait for it to fire.
Map the pullback's staircase.Mark each higher low. The most recent one is the CHoCH level.
Did price sweep an internal high as it tapped the zone?The new high becomes the protected high.
Did a candle close below the most recent higher low with displacement?That is the CHoCH. It should leave an imbalance.
Does it pay at least 1:2 to the SSL?Sell limit at the bottom edge of the small supply, stop above the protected high, target the low. Cancel if the protected high breaks or price reaches halfway to target unfilled.
For longs, mirror both lists: demand for supply, lows for highs, protected low for protected high.

entries.h: Where each trade sits
entries.t:
In the case studies
Where each trade sits
All eleven trades on this site waited for a lower-timeframe shift before entering, so all eleven are confirmation entries. None is a pure aggressive entry.
| Case | The larger location | The confirmation | Entered from
| USD/JPY long (4H) | 4H demand zone | 30m MSS after a sweep | 15m order block
| XAU/USD short | Swept 1H internal highs in premium | 15m MSS after three sweeps | 15m order block
| GBP/JPY long (15m) | Swept higher-timeframe low | 15m MSS, then BoS | 15m order block
| BTC/USD long (15m) | Swept low (no higher timeframe shown) | 15m MSS, then BoS | 15m order block
| AUD/USD long | H4 demand zone in discount | M15 MSS after two sweeps | M15 demand zone
| BTC/USD long (1H) | 4H sweep and shift, 1H demand below | 1H MSS after equal lows are swept | 1H demand zone
| GBP/AUD long | 1H demand that caused a BoS | 15m MSS after the range low is swept | 15m demand zone
| USD/JPY long (1H) | 30m demand after a 1H MSS | 15m MSS after a sweep at the zone | 15m demand zone
| GBP/USD short | 15m supply after a 1H BoS down | 15m MSS after two highs are swept in the zone | New 15m supply zone
| AUD/USD short | 1H order block after a 1H MSS down | 15m MSS and BoS after a high is swept in the block | 15m order block
| GBP/JPY long (5m) | 1H order block, then the 15m order block | 5m MSS after a low is swept in the 15m block | 5m order block
A confirmation pattern can still fail if it prints above the zone instead of at it. See Inducement.
The aggressive version of the first USD/JPY trade would have been a buy limit at the top of the 4H demand zone with a stop below it. It would have filled and worked, with a much wider stop. That comparison is the trade-off on this page in one example.
Keep this in proportion
Neither model is the better one in general. In principle, aggressive entries lose more often and pay more when they win, while confirmation entries lose less often, pay less and miss some moves. Which comes out ahead depends on the market and on how you execute. Backtest both on the same set of zones and compare total R, not win rate.

entries.h: Introduction
entries.t:
Concept
The full sequence: structure, sweep, shift, imbalance, order block
One long trade, shown one element at a time. Structure gives the direction. A liquidity sweep ends the pullback. A market structure shift confirms the turn. The imbalance and order block give the entry. Every case study on this site is a version of this sequence, so this page works as the short form of the whole method.
Drawn as a long
No pair or timeframe named
Target reached · ≈ 1:3
From the post
“Instead of guessing where the market is going, learn to read the structural story step-by-step.”
1 · Market structure
2 · Liquidity sweep
3 · Structure shift
4 · IMB + OB
5 · Entry + target
6 · Result
Everything as one
Entry, SL & TP
Repeatable steps
Is it all you need?
How to read this page
X marks a liquidity sweep. SSL and BSL are sell-side and buy-side liquidity. IMB is an imbalance and OB an order block. The slides carry titles only and show no pair, timeframe, price or time. The explanations are my reading of the charts. Reward-to-risk is measured from the position box.

entries.h: Market structure: which way is the trend?
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart in an uptrend. Price breaks three successive highs, two of them labelled BoS, with a higher low between each. After the last break price drifts lower.
Slide 1 — “Market Structure.”
Part 1 · Direction
Market structure: which way is the trend?
What the slide shows
Three breaks of structure upward. Each time, price closes above the previous high. Two are labelled BoS and the first has a line without a label.
A higher low between each break. One pullback has a long wick down. It did not close below the prior low.
After the last break, a drift lower. Small candles, no break of a low.
Why it comes first
Higher highs and higher lows mean the trend is up. That decides the side: look for longs only. It also decides how to read what comes next. The drift lower is a pullback in an uptrend until a low is closed below.
Rule to carry forward
Before anything else, mark the last break of structure and the low it came from. Trade in the direction of that break.

entries.h: Liquidity sweep: the pullback takes the low
entries.t:
Chart: Wider candle chart. After a break of structure upward, price declines for a long time. Near the end it spikes up and reverses sharply. A wick then runs below the low the break of structure started from, marked X, and closes back above it.
Slide 2 — “Liquidity Sweep.”
Part 2 · Liquidity
Liquidity sweep: the pullback takes the low
What the slide shows
The BoS at the left. One large bullish candle. The base it launched from is the low under the X line.
A long, slow pullback. Price gives back the whole move, step by step.
A spike up and full reversal. Late in the pullback price jumps and is sold straight back. The slide does not label it.
The sweep (X). A wick runs below the low the BoS came from and closes back above it.
Why it matters
The low under a break of structure is where buyers from that move keep their stops. A wick through it takes those stops and fills larger buy orders. The candle closing back above is what makes it a sweep.
This low is also the one that must hold
The low that launched a BoS is the protected low. A close below it would break the bullish structure from slide 1. Here only a wick went through. At the moment of the sweep you cannot yet know which it is. That is why the next step exists.

entries.h: Market structure shift: proof the sweep was a sweep
entries.t:
Chart: Close-up candle chart. Price spikes up and collapses, makes a low, bounces and makes a small high. A wick then sweeps below the old low. The next bullish candle closes above the small high, labelled MSS.
Slide 3 — “Market Structure Shift.”
Part 3 · Confirmation
Market structure shift: proof the sweep was a sweep
What the slide shows
The line at the bottom. The old low from slide 2.
The sweep wick. It goes through that line and comes back.
The MSS. A large bullish candle closes above the last small high of the decline.
Why it matters
During the pullback the short-term trend was down: lower highs, lower lows. The MSS is the first close above one of those lower highs. Coming straight after a sweep, it says sellers could not hold price under the low and buyers have taken over.
Rule to carry forward
After a sweep, mark the last lower high. Do nothing until a candle closes above it. A sweep with no shift is not a signal.

entries.h: Imbalance and order block: where to enter
entries.t:
Chart: The same close-up with more labels. A BSL line sits far above. The sweep wick low is labelled SSL. The candle that made the MSS is marked with an imbalance arrow, and an order block box is drawn at its base.
Slide 4 — “IMB + OB.”
Part 4 · The zone
Imbalance and order block: where to enter
What is marked
IMB. The MSS candle moved so fast that it left an imbalance. The arrow points at it.
OB. A box at the base of that candle, covering the last small candles before it.
SSL. The low of the sweep wick, under the order block. The sell-side liquidity there has been taken.
BSL. A line far above, with a dashed line just under it. Buy-side liquidity that has not been taken.
Why it matters
The imbalance shows the move had force. The order block is where that force started, so it is where unfilled buy orders are most likely to remain. The two together turn “price should go up” into a price to buy at.
The slide does not show which high the BSL line is drawn from. I assume it is a high from the uptrend on slide 1.
Rule to carry forward
When the MSS candle closes, draw the order block at its base and check there is an imbalance above it. No imbalance, no trade.

entries.h: Entry and target: three prices fixed in advance
entries.t:
Chart: The same chart with a position box. The entry is at the top edge of the order block, the stop is at the sweep low labelled SSL, and the target is at the BSL line far above.
Slide 5 — “Entry + Target.”
Part 5 · The order
Entry and target: three prices fixed in advance
What is marked
Entry. The top edge of the order block.
Stop. The bottom of the grey box is level with the SSL line, the low of the sweep wick.
Target. The BSL line.
Reading the box
The target is about three times the stop. Price has only just shifted and has not come back yet. This is a resting limit order.
The stop covers the whole order block and the wick under it. That is wider than a stop just under the block, and it is why the ratio is 1:3 and not higher.

entries.h: Result: an edge fill, then a straight run
entries.t:
Chart: Result. After the shift price pushes up, returns to the top edge of the order block and holds there for several candles with small wicks into it. It then rallies in a nearly straight line to the BSL line, wicks through it, and falls back.
Slide 6 — “Result.”
Result
Result: an edge fill, then a straight run
What happened
A push up first. After the MSS, several large candles carried price higher.
The return. Price came back and sat on the top edge of the order block for several candles. Wicks dipped a short way into it.
The rally. A nearly straight climb to the BSL line.
The target. Three wicks went through the line. Then price fell back hard.
What to take from it
The fill was at the edge. An order placed deeper in the block might not have filled.
The stop was never approached.
Price turned down right at the BSL. Taking profit at the liquidity, not beyond it, was correct here.

entries.h: Five elements, five questions
entries.t:
Everything as one
Five elements, five questions
Chart: Cover slide: Market Structure + Liquidity Sweep + MSS + IMB + OB is all you need, showing the finished long.
Cover — “Market Structure + Liquidity Sweep + MSS + IMB + OB is all you need.”
Each element answers one question. The order matters. Each answer is only useful if the one before it was yes.
| Element | Question it answers | On this chart | Without it
| 1. Market structure | Which side do I trade? | Higher highs and higher lows: long | You buy sweeps in a downtrend
| 2. Liquidity sweep | Has the pullback done its job? | A wick through the low under the BoS | You buy before the stops are taken and become the liquidity
| 3. MSS | Was that a sweep or a real break? | A close above the last lower high | You buy a falling market on a guess
| 4. IMB | Did the shift have force? | The MSS candle left an imbalance | You trade a weak break that often fails
| 5. OB | At what price do I enter? | The base of the MSS candle | You chase and the stop becomes too wide
1 · STRUCTURE
An uptrend with breaks of structure. Longs only.
2 · SWEEP
The pullback runs a wick under the low the last break came from and closes back above.
3 · SHIFT
A candle closes above the last lower high of the pullback.
4 · IMB + OB
That candle leaves an imbalance. The order block is drawn at its base.
5 · ORDER
Buy limit at the top of the order block, stop under the sweep low, target the buy-side liquidity. About 1:3.
THE LOGIC IN ONE SENTENCE
In an uptrend, wait for the pullback to sweep a low and shift back up with force, then buy the origin of that shift toward the high.

entries.h: Entry, stop loss and take profit
entries.t:
Order placement
Entry, stop loss and take profit
Entry
Buy limit at the top edge of the order block.
The order block is the base of the candle that made the MSS, under the imbalance.
Place the order as soon as that candle closes.
Here price returned to the edge and went little further. The edge is the price that fills most often.
Stop loss
Below the sweep low (the SSL line), plus a buffer.
The grey box ends at the sweep wick. Put the stop a little beyond it.
If that low breaks, the sweep was a real break and the uptrend from slide 1 is in question.
Do not put it just under the order block to improve the ratio. Deep fills are common in the case studies.
Take profit
The BSL line. About 3R.
Untouched buy-side liquidity above a prior high.
Price wicked through it and reversed. Set the order a little before the line.
If the distance from the order block to the BSL is under twice the stop, skip the trade.

entries.h: Step-by-step for the next trade
entries.t:
Repeatable strategy
Step-by-step for the next trade
Written for longs. For shorts, mirror it. A “no” at any step ends the process.
Is structure making higher highs and higher lows?Mark the last BoS and the low it launched from.
Mark the liquidity.The low under the BoS is the sell-side. The nearest untaken high above is the buy-side and the target.
Has the pullback swept that low?A wick below and a close back above. A close below it ends the long idea.
Has a candle closed above the last lower high?That is the MSS.
Did that candle leave an imbalance?If the break was slow and overlapping, pass.
Draw the order block at the base of that candle.Buy limit at its top edge. Stop under the sweep low. Target the buy-side liquidity.
Does it pay at least 1:2?If not, skip it.
Size, place, hold, record.Risk 0.5–1%. Exit at target or stop.
The longer version, with timeframes, order rules and risk rules, is the daily routine in the playbook.

entries.h: Is it really all you need?
entries.t:
A fair test of the headline
Is it really all you need?
The five elements are the core of every trade on this site. The comparison table in the playbook shows the same sweep, shift and zone in all eleven case studies. The headline still leaves things out.
What the five elements cover
Direction.
When the pullback is finished.
Evidence that the turn is real.
The entry price.
Where the idea is wrong, which gives the stop.
What they do not cover
The target. Even this post adds a sixth thing, the BSL. See types of liquidity.
Which zone is the real one. A sweep and shift above the true zone is a trap. See inducement.
Timeframe alignment. Most case studies read direction on a higher timeframe than the entry.
Risk. Position size, a minimum ratio and a daily loss limit.
News and session. None of the five says when not to trade.
Keep this in proportion
This is one winning example with no pair, timeframe or date. It shows what the sequence looks like when it works. It says nothing about how often it works. The same five elements appear on charts that then fail, and the stop under the sweep low exists for those.

entries.h: Introduction
entries.t:
Concept
Inducement: a liquidity trap
After a sweep and a structure shift, price often pauses and leaves a small, tidy zone close to current price. It has a break of structure, a pullback and sometimes an imbalance. It looks like the entry. Its real job is to collect buyers and their stops, so that price has something to take on its way to the zone the move actually came from.
Drawn as longs
Concept, no pair named
Mirror for shorts
From the post's closing slide
“The first setup that looks valid is often not the best one. The better entry usually comes after the trap, not before it.”
1 · Two zones
2 · Why it looks clean
3 · Early entries stopped
4 · The real zone
Telling them apart
Entry, SL & TP
Repeatable steps
In the case studies
How to read this page
The slides show one candle chart at three moments, plus one line drawing of the same idea. No pair, timeframe or price scale is given. X marks a liquidity sweep. $$$ marks resting liquidity. BSL is buy-side liquidity. Where I give a reward-to-risk figure it is measured from the drawn boxes.

entries.h: One move, two zones
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. A range low is swept (X), a large bullish candle breaks structure (MSS), price pauses briefly and continues up. Two demand zones are marked: a lower one at the base of the large candle and an upper one at the pause, with a liquidity line under the upper one.
Slide 1 — “Inducement: A Liquidity Trap.”
Step 1 · The setup
One move, two zones
What the chart shows
A range, then a sweep (X). Price drifts sideways. A wick runs under the earlier low of the range and is rejected.
MSS on one large candle. A single bullish candle closes above the range high. This is the displacement.
The lower zone. Drawn at the base of that candle, where the move began. Price has not been back to it.
A short pause, then continuation. Two small candles pull back a little. The next candle breaks to a new high.
The upper zone. Drawn around that pause. The line under it is marked $$$: the low of the pause, where stops will sit.
The question the slide is asking
Both boxes are demand zones by the usual definition. The upper one is closer, it formed after the shift and it led to a new high. The lower one is further away and needs a deeper pullback. Which do you buy?
The label gives it away. The upper zone has liquidity marked directly beneath it. The lower one has nothing beneath it except the sweep that has already happened.
Rule to carry forward
When two zones are stacked, ask which one is the origin of the displacement that broke structure. That is the real zone. A zone formed after the break, on the way up, is a candidate for inducement.

entries.h: Why the trap looks like a clean entry
entries.t:
Chart: Line diagram. Price rallies from a higher-timeframe order block, breaks structure, and returns to a zone labelled Inducement where it sweeps a low and shifts up; a long is taken and then stopped out as price falls through the zone. Price then sweeps a low inside the higher-timeframe order block, shifts up, and a second long from a lower-timeframe order block reaches the target.
Slide 2 — “A small structure forms. A BOS, a pullback, maybe a IBM. It looks like a clean entry.”
Step 2 · The trap in detail
Why the trap looks like a clean entry
This drawing shows two trades with the same pattern. The first loses. The second wins. Read it left to right.
The first trade: at the inducement zone
Price leaves the HTF order block and breaks structure (BoS). The pullback low that led to the break is boxed and labelled Inducement, with $$$ under it.
Price returns to that zone.
Inside it, a small low is swept (X) and structure shifts up (MSS). That is a complete confirmation pattern.
A long is taken. The first position box: entry at the top of the zone, stop just under the $$$ low.
Price falls straight through. The $$$ low and the stop are taken.
The second trade: at the HTF order block
Price carries on down into the HTF OB.
The same pattern prints again. A low is swept (X), then an MSS.
A long is taken from the LTF order block that the shift leaves behind, with the stop under the sweep low.
Price rallies to the earlier high. About three times the risk on the drawing.
Why this matters
This is the uncomfortable part. The first trade was not careless. It waited for a sweep and a shift, which is exactly what the confirmation model asks for. It still lost, because of where it happened: above the higher-timeframe zone, with a clean low underneath it and the real zone still untouched below that.
Rule to carry forward
A confirmation pattern is only as good as its location. Sweep plus shift inside the higher-timeframe zone is a signal. The same pattern above the zone, with liquidity resting beneath it, is bait.
The slide text says “IBM”. From the other posts I read it as IMB, imbalance.

entries.h: Traders enter early and are stopped
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart continued. Price has made a new high and fallen back into the upper zone. A long position is drawn from the top of the upper zone with its stop under the liquidity line; the last candle's wick goes below that stop. An imbalance separates the upper and lower zones, and a BSL line marks the target above.
Slide 3 — “Traders enter early. Price goes against them and takes their stops.”
Step 3 · The trap closes
Traders enter early and are stopped
What happened
Price made its new high and turned. A run of bearish candles brings it back to the upper zone.
The early long. The position box shows the trade most people take: buy the top of the upper zone, stop just under the $$$ low, target the BSL line at the top.
Price stalls inside the zone. A few small candles. It looks like the zone is holding.
One candle drops through the $$$ line. Its wick goes below the stop. The early longs are out.
An imbalance lies below (IMB). The gap left by the displacement candle sits between the two zones and has not been filled.
What gave it away beforehand
An unfilled imbalance directly beneath the upper zone.
An untouched zone at the origin of the move, beneath the imbalance.
A single obvious low under the upper zone for stops to gather at.
A shallow pullback. The upper zone is roughly at the middle of the leg; the lower zone is in the discount half.
Rule to carry forward
Before buying a zone, look underneath it. If there is an unfilled imbalance and an untouched origin zone below, expect price to go there, and expect the stops under your zone to be taken on the way.

entries.h: Only then does price reach the real zone
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart continued. Price falls through the upper zone and the imbalance, a wick touches the top of the lower zone, and price then rallies up to and through the BSL line.
Slide 4 — “Only then does price reach the real zone. This is where the move starts.”
Step 4 · The real entry
Only then does price reach the real zone
What happened
Price kept falling after the stops were taken. It filled the imbalance.
A wick touched the top of the lower zone. Just the edge, then a close back above.
Price turned and rallied. Back up through the upper zone, to the earlier high, then on to the BSL line and through it.
The position box still on the slide is the early trade from slide 3, shown for comparison. Its target was reached in the end, but only after its stop had been hit.
What to take from it
The early traders had the direction and the target right. They lost on location alone.
The fill at the real zone was a wick. A limit order at the top edge filled. Waiting to watch a reaction would have meant chasing.
The trap supplied the fuel. Stops from the early longs are sell orders. They gave larger buyers something to fill against at a better price.
Rule to carry forward
Put the limit order at the origin zone and treat everything above it as liquidity. The better entry comes after the trap, not before it.

entries.h: Inducement or the real zone?
entries.t:
Telling them apart
Inducement or the real zone?
The slides show what inducement looks like after the fact. The table below turns that into checks you can run beforehand. The first two rows come from the slides. The rest are my reading.
| Check | Inducement | Real zone
| What is underneath it? | A clean low with stops ($$$), and often an unfilled imbalance | The sweep low. The liquidity there has already been taken
| How did it form? | A pause or small pullback after structure had already broken | The base of the displacement that broke structure
| Where is it in the leg? | Shallow, around or above the midpoint | Deep, in the discount half
| Where is it relative to the HTF zone? | Above it. Price has left the HTF zone and not come back | Inside it
| Is another untouched zone below? | Yes | No. It is the last zone before the sweep low
| How obvious is it? | Very. It is the first thing everyone sees | Less. It needs a deeper pullback that feels like the move is failing
The first zone sometimes holds
None of these checks is certain. In a strong trend price can turn at the shallow zone and never come back for the deep one. If you always wait for the origin zone you will miss those moves. That is the price of avoiding the trap, and it is why the post says “often” and “usually”, not “always”.

entries.h: Entry, stop loss and take profit
entries.t:
Order placement
Entry, stop loss and take profit
For the trade at the real zone. The candle slides do not draw this position, so the placements follow the line drawing on slide 2 and the case studies.
Entry
Buy limit at the top edge of the origin zone.
The origin zone is the base of the displacement candle that made the MSS.
On the candle chart only a wick reached it. A limit at the edge filled.
Stricter version, from the line drawing: wait for a sweep and MSS inside the zone and buy the LTF order block it leaves.
Stop loss
Below the origin zone, under the sweep low.
The sweep low (X) is where the whole move began. If it breaks, the idea is finished.
In the line drawing the stop sits at the low of the sweep inside the HTF OB.
Never under the inducement low. That is the level price is being drawn to.
Take profit
The high above, or the BSL beyond it.
The line drawing targets the high made before the pullback, at about 1:3.
The candle chart marks a BSL line higher up, which price also reached.
The entry is lower than the early trader's and the target is the same, so the deeper zone can pay more per unit of risk.

entries.h: Step-by-step for the next trade
entries.t:
Repeatable strategy
Step-by-step for the next trade
Written for longs. For shorts, mirror it.
Find the sweep and the shift.A low taken and rejected, then a displacement candle closing above the prior high.
Mark the origin zone.The base of the displacement candle, above the sweep low. Place the buy limit at its top edge.
Mark every zone and low that forms above it afterwards.Pauses, small pullbacks, first higher lows. Label each one as liquidity, not as an entry.
Check what lies between price and the origin zone.An unfilled imbalance or an untaken low means price has a reason to come down.
If price reacts at an upper zone, do nothing.Even if it prints a sweep and a shift there. Note the new low it leaves.
If price runs to target without you, accept it.Cancel the order. Record it as a missed trade.
When price reaches the origin zone, the order fills.Stop under the sweep low, target at the high above. At least 1:2, risk 0.5–1%.

entries.h: Where this has already appeared
entries.t:
In the case studies
Where this has already appeared
| Case | The inducement | What price did
| AUD/USD long | The IDM low after the shift, then a bounce above the zone that left a $$$ low | Took both, then filled deep in the M15 demand about 13 hours after the shift
| BTC/USD long | A sharp pullback that turned just above the order block, leaving a $$ low | Rallied to a new high, then came back through that low deep into the order block
| GBP/JPY long | A wick low and a cluster of lows sitting above the order block | Swept both, then one wick tapped the order block about 12 hours after the shift
| GBP/AUD long | The IDM low left just after the shift | Took it, filled the imbalance and touched the 15m demand about 3 hours after the shift
| USD/JPY long (1H) | Twice: the 30m pullback low before the BoS, then the 15m pullback low after the shift | Took the first on the way to the 30m demand and the second on the way to the 15m demand
In all five, the low that looked like support was taken before the zone was reached. The AUD/USD case is the closest match to this page: it uses the IDM label and nearly the same slide captions.
Compare this with the entry models. The confirmation entry asks for a sweep and a shift before entering. This page adds the condition that makes it work: the sweep and shift have to happen at the zone, not above it.
Keep this in proportion
Every example on this site was chosen because the deep zone was reached and held. To know how often that happens, you need the other outcomes too: the times the shallow zone held and the trade was missed, and the times the origin zone was reached and failed. Log all three when you backtest.

entries.h: Introduction
entries.t:
Concept
Types of liquidity
Liquidity is where stop orders and breakout orders collect. They collect where many traders look at the same thing: a swing high, two lows at the same price, a line across the highs, the edge of a range, the high of the last session. Price often visits those places first and makes its lasting move afterwards. This page covers six such places, in two parts, and how to trade around them.
Concept, no pair named
Buy-side: stops above highs
Sell-side: stops below lows
From the post
“Many traders watch the same places. They use the same lines and take the same early entries. That is why price often goes to these places first, before it makes its real move.”
1.1 · Swing high & low
1.2 · Relative equal highs
1.3 · Relative equal lows
1.4 · Equal highs
1.5 · Equal lows
Three jobs
2.1 · Trendline, downtrend
2.2 · Trendline, uptrend
2.3 · Range

How to read this page
The page follows two posts, “Types of Liquidity” Part 1 and Part 2. The slides give no pair, timeframe or price scale, and they draw no entries, stops or targets. $$$ marks resting liquidity. The order placement further down is my application of the site's playbook to these slides, not something the post shows.

entries.h: Liquidity at single levels: swings and equal highs and lows
entries.t:
Part 1
Liquidity at single levels: swings and equal highs and lows
The simplest liquidity sits at one price: above a high or below a low. The more times price has turned at that level, the more stops are stacked beyond it.

entries.h: Swing high and swing low
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. A rally makes a swing high and pulls back. Later a wick spikes above the swing high and price drops sharply, all the way to the swing low at the start of the rally, where a wick goes just below it.
Part 1, slide 1 — “The most obvious turning points on the chart. Stop losses gather above swing highs and below swing lows.”
1.1
Swing high and swing low
A swing high is a peak with lower candles on both sides. A swing low is the reverse. They are the first thing anyone marks on a chart, so they are where the most stops sit.
Above the swing high: buy stops from sellers, and buy orders from breakout traders.
Below the swing low: sell stops from buyers, and sell orders from breakout traders.
What price did: one wick went above the swing high and failed. Price then fell the whole way to the swing low and put a wick through that too.
One chart shows both jobs. The swing high was the liquidity that was taken before the move. The swing low was where the move went.
Rule from this slide
Mark the swing high and swing low of the leg you are trading. One of them is where a sweep can start a trade. The other is the target.

entries.h: Relative equal highs
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Two highs, marked with arrows, turn at nearly the same level. A third push goes clearly above the line and price then falls back sharply.
Part 1, slide 2 — “Highs that are close, but not exactly equal. The third one goes above the line, then price comes back down.”
1.2
Relative equal highs
Two highs that turn at nearly the same price. They do not have to match to the pip. Traders see resistance and sell it, with stops just above.
The two touches: marked with arrows. Each one turned price down.
The third: price goes clearly above the line. The breakout does not hold.
Afterwards: large bearish candles bring price back under the line and well below it.
Just before the third push, a long wick dipped under the earlier lows and recovered. The slide does not label it. I read it as the sell-side being taken first, as on the trendline slides in Part 2.
Rule from this slide
After two touches of a level, do not sell the third touch with a stop just above. That stop is the liquidity. Wait for the push through and see whether it holds.

entries.h: Relative equal lows
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Two lows, marked with arrows, turn at nearly the same level. A third dip goes below the line and price then climbs back above it and rallies.
Part 1, slide 3 — “Lows that are close, but not exactly equal. The third one goes below the line, then price comes back up.”
1.3
Relative equal lows
The mirror image. Two lows at nearly the same price look like support. Buyers enter there with stops just below.
The two touches: marked with arrows.
The third: a candle goes below the line. Its wick reaches further still.
Afterwards: price climbs back above the line and rallies to the dotted level above.
This is the pattern behind most of the long entries on this site: lows that look like support are taken, then price turns.

entries.h: Equal highs
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Two highs at exactly the same level are marked with arrows. Price falls a long way, recovers in a V, pushes above the equal highs with wicks, and starts to come back under them.
Part 1, slide 4 — “Two highs at the same level. Then price goes above it, and comes back down.”
1.4
Equal highs
Two highs at exactly the same price. This is the cleanest version, often called a double top. The cleaner the level, the more traders use it, and the more stops sit above it.
The two highs: side by side at the left, marked with arrows.
The return: price falls a long way, then recovers the whole drop.
The take: wicks go above the level. The last candles are back under it.
The chart stops early
The slide says price “comes back down”. The chart ends only a little under the level, right after the take. The larger fall is not shown. At this point on a live chart you would not know yet whether it was a sweep or a pause before a breakout.

entries.h: Equal lows
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Two lows at the same level are marked with arrows. Price rallies, tops out, then falls below the equal lows. The last candle is bullish and closes back up to a dotted level just above them.
Part 1, slide 5 — “Two lows at the same level. Then price goes below it, and comes back up.”
1.5
Equal lows
Two lows at the same price: a double bottom. Buyers treat it as strong support. Their stops sit just under it.
The two lows: at the left, marked with arrows. Price rallied a long way from the second.
The take: the rally rolls over and price falls through the level. It goes some distance below, with candle bodies under the line.
The return: one bullish candle closes back above the level, at the dotted line.
Price spent several candles below the level here. A sweep is not always a single wick. What counts is that price gets back above and then shifts structure.
Rule for all four equal-level slides
Equal and near-equal highs and lows are targets first. Price is drawn to them. They become entry areas only after they are taken and price has come back through.

entries.h: Liquidity has more than one job
entries.t:
Part 1, closing slide
Liquidity has more than one job
Chart: Text slide: Liquidity has more than one job. It is where price wants to go. It is fuel for big players to fill their orders. It can also be a target for your take profit.
Part 1, slide 6.
1 · A DESTINATION
“It is where price wants to go.”
Untouched highs and lows pull price toward them. Before a trade, ask which pool is nearest in each direction.
2 · FUEL
“It is fuel for big players to fill their orders.”
A large buyer needs sellers. Stops under a low are sell orders. Taking them lets the buyer fill, which is why reversals so often start with a sweep.
3 · A TARGET
“It can also be a target for your take profit.”
If price is drawn to a pool, that is where to exit. Place the take profit just before the level, not beyond it.

entries.h: Liquidity along lines and blocks of time: trendlines, ranges and sessions
entries.t:
Part 2
Liquidity along lines and blocks of time: trendlines, ranges and sessions
The same idea, spread over more than one price. Stops follow a diagonal line, sit on both sides of a range, or collect beyond the high and low of a session.

entries.h: Trendline liquidity above a downtrend
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. After a rally, price makes three lower highs joined by a dotted descending line marked with dollar signs. Price falls to a new low, then rallies through the line and above all the earlier highs before pulling back.
Part 2, slide 1 — “In a downtrend, sellers draw a line over the highs. They place their stops just above it. Price often breaks above the line first, takes those stops, then moves up.”
2.1
Trendline liquidity above a downtrend
Three lower highs line up. Anyone can join them with a line, and many do. They sell each touch and put the stop just above the line. Every touch adds more stops, so the liquidity above the line grows the longer the line holds.
What is above the line: buy stops from sellers, plus buy orders from traders waiting for a trendline break.
What price did: it rallied through the line and through every high behind it in one leg.
What came just before: a sharp drop to a new low under the earlier lows. The slide does not label it, but that drop took the sell-side first. The rally started from there.
Look at the last candles
After the break, price falls back a long way and the chart ends. The slide says price “moves up”, and it did go up through the line. Whether it kept going is not shown. Treat a trendline as a place price is drawn to, and take profit there. Do not assume the break continues.

entries.h: Trendline liquidity under an uptrend
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Price rises in steps. A dotted ascending line joins the lows, with dollar signs beneath it. At the top a long wick spikes above the highs, then large bearish candles fall through the line and continue far below it.
Part 2, slide 2 — “In an uptrend, buyers draw a line under the lows. They place their stops just below it. Price often breaks below the line first, takes those stops, then moves down.”
2.2
Trendline liquidity under an uptrend
The mirror image. Rising lows are joined by a line. Buyers buy each touch and place stops under it. Those stops are sell orders, and they sit in a neat diagonal row.
What is below the line: sell stops from buyers, plus sell orders from breakout traders.
What price did: large bearish candles cut through the line and kept falling, past the low the line started from.
What came just before: one long wick above the recent highs that closed back down. Again unlabelled, and again it is a sweep of the opposite side before the move.
What both trendline slides share
In both, price first takes liquidity on one side with a wick or a fast drop, then travels to the trendline liquidity on the other side. The trendline is the destination. The sweep on the opposite side is the place to look for the entry.

entries.h: Range liquidity
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart. Price moves sideways between a high and a low, each marked with a line and dollar signs. One large bullish candle breaks above the range high, the next candles reverse, fall through the range low and continue down.
Part 2, slide 3 — “In a range, stops sit outside both sides. Price often takes one side first, before it chooses a direction.”
2.3
Range liquidity
Price moves sideways between a high and a low. Traders who sell the top put stops above the high. Traders who buy the bottom put stops below the low. Breakout traders place orders at both. So a range has liquidity on each side.
The take: one large bullish candle closes above the range high. It looks like a breakout.
The failure: the next candles are bearish and bring price straight back inside the range.
The move: price falls through the whole range and through the low on the other side.
The breakout candle here closed above the high, not just a wick. That matters. A close beyond the level is not proof of a real break. What settles it is what the next few candles do.
Rule from this slide
Do not trade the first break of a range. Wait to see whether price holds outside it or comes back in. If it comes back in, the opposite side of the range becomes the target.

entries.h: Session highs and lows
entries.t:
Chart: Candle chart with three shaded blocks. In the Asia block price falls, leaving an Asia high and an Asia low. In the London block price moves sideways, leaving a London high and a London low above the Asia low. In the New York block price first drops below the London low and the Asia low, then rallies above the London high and the Asia high to a New York high, and falls back.
Part 2, slide 4 — “Every session leaves a high and a low behind. Traders see them and place stops just beyond. A later session often runs through them first, then makes its real move.”
2.4
Session highs and lows
Each trading session is a block of time with its own high and low. Those levels are easy to see and easy to mark, so stops collect beyond them like any other high or low.
| Session | What it did on the slide | What it left
| Asia | Fell from the top of the chart | Asia high far above, Asia low below
| London | Moved sideways. Its low stayed above the Asia low | London high and London low, both inside the Asia range
| New York | Dropped first, through the London low and the Asia low. Then rallied through the London high and the Asia high | New York low and New York high
New York took the lows of both earlier sessions first. That drop was the visit to liquidity. The rally that followed was the larger move, and its targets were the London high and then the Asia high.
The slide also shows price falling back after the New York high. That high is now liquidity for the next session.
Session hours
The slide gives no clock times. As a rough guide in UTC: Asia about 00:00–09:00, London about 07:00–16:00, New York about 12:00–21:00. For Nairobi, add three hours. These shift by an hour with daylight saving in London and New York, and brokers define them differently. Check the session indicator on your own platform.

entries.h: What price does after it takes the liquidity
entries.t:
The other half
What price does after it takes the liquidity
Chart: Text slide: Some liquidity is easy to see. Some looks like a setup. Knowing where it is only gets you halfway. What price does after it takes it is the other half.
Part 2, slide 5 — the closing slide.
Marking liquidity tells you where price is likely to go. It does not tell you what happens when it arrives. There are two outcomes, and the candles after the take show which one you have.
| Check | Sweep (trade the reversal) | Real break (stand aside or trade with it)
| Where do the next candles close? | Back inside the level within a few candles | Outside it, candle after candle
| Does structure shift back? | Yes. A displacement candle breaks the last swing the other way (MSS) | No. Pullbacks stop at or beyond the old level
| What is left behind? | A fresh zone with an imbalance beside it, pointing back into the range | A fresh zone pointing in the direction of the break
| Does the higher timeframe agree? | The take ran into an HTF zone, or against the HTF trend | The take is in the direction of the HTF trend with room to run
The first three rows can be seen on the slides. The fourth is my addition and comes from the case studies, where each sweep happened at a higher-timeframe zone.
“Often” is not “always”
Every slide says price “often” takes the liquidity first. Real breakouts happen too, and from the level alone the two look identical. That is why the entry on this site comes after the shift and not at the level. A sell limit resting at a range high is a bet that the break fails, placed before there is any evidence.

entries.h: Entry, stop loss and take profit
entries.t:
Order placement
Entry, stop loss and take profit
For a short after buy-side liquidity is taken, as on the range slide. For a long after sell-side is taken, mirror every line. The slides draw no positions, so these placements follow the playbook used in the case studies.
Entry
Sell limit at the bottom edge of the supply zone left by the shift.
First price must take the high and come back under it.
Then a displacement candle must close below the last swing low (MSS), leaving an imbalance.
The supply zone is the last up candle, or small base, before that displacement. Rest the order at its near edge.
Stop loss
Above the sweep high, plus spread and a small buffer.
The sweep high is where the liquidity was taken. If price goes back above it, the break was real.
Not at the old range high or on the trendline. Those are the levels everyone else uses, which is why they were swept.
If that stop makes the trade smaller than 1:2 to the target, skip it.
Take profit
The untouched liquidity on the other side.
Swing or equal highs and lows: the level itself. Set the order just before it.
Range: the opposite side of the range.
Sessions: the nearest untaken session low, then the next one.
Trendline: the lows the line is drawn through. Take profit at the first one if a higher-timeframe demand zone sits in between.
Two uses for every level you mark
Liquidity that has just been taken and rejected gives the entry area. Liquidity that is still untouched in the direction of the trade gives the target. Before placing an order, name both. If you cannot name the liquidity that was taken, there is no entry. If you cannot name the liquidity ahead, there is no target.

entries.h: Step-by-step for each day
entries.t:
Repeatable strategy
Step-by-step for each day
A marking routine to run before the session you trade. It feeds the daily routine in the playbook.
Mark the swing high and swing low of the current leg.On the timeframe you take direction from, and one below it.
Mark equal and near-equal highs and lows.Two or more turns at about the same price. These hold the most stops.
Mark the previous sessions' highs and lows.Asia high and low before London. Asia and London highs and lows before New York. Add yesterday's high and low.
Mark any range.Three or more turns between the same high and low. Draw both sides.
Mark any trendline with three clean touches.Label it as liquidity. Do not buy or sell the touches.
Note which levels have already been taken.A taken level is finished. Only untouched levels are targets.
Check the higher-timeframe bias and zones.The strongest sweep takes liquidity on the side the bias is pushing away from, at an HTF zone. Example: a low taken inside HTF demand in an uptrend.
Wait for price to take a marked level.Set an alert at each level. Do nothing until one triggers.
Watch the next candles.Back inside and a shift with an imbalance: plan the trade. Holding outside: leave it alone.
Place the limit order at the zone the shift left.Stop beyond the sweep extreme. Target the nearest untouched level on the other side. At least 1:2, risk 0.5–1%.
Log it either way.Which type of liquidity, sweep or real break, and what price did afterwards.

entries.h: Where this has already appeared
entries.t:
In the case studies
Where this has already appeared
| Case | Type | What price did
| GBP/AUD long | Range liquidity | About nine hours of 15m range above the 1H demand. The range low was swept, then one candle shifted structure up
| BTC/USD long (1H) | Range liquidity | The lows of a 4H range were swept before the 4H shift, and the high above became the target
| USD/JPY long (1H) | Trendline liquidity | Rising 30m lows marked $$ sat above the 30m demand. Price later fell through them to reach the zone
| GBP/USD short | Trendline liquidity | Two rising lows joined by a $$$ line under the bounce. The short targeted the upper of the two
| BTC/USD long (1H) | Equal lows | Equal lows on the 1H were swept into demand, then the 1H shifted up
| GBP/JPY long | Equal or near-equal lows | A double low on the 15m was swept before the shift
| XAU/USD short | Swing high | The 4H took an old high, then shifted down
| The full sequence | Swing low and swing high | The swing low under the last BoS was swept for the entry. The high above (BSL) was the target
The first two used the range the same way as slide 3: one side taken first, the other side as the target. The USD/JPY case shows liquidity under a rising line being taken on the way to the zone. None of the case studies so far labels a session high or low. That type is untested on this site, so backtest it before giving it the same weight.
Related: inducement is the liquidity that forms after a shift, close to price. This page covers the liquidity that is already on the chart before the setup begins.
Keep this in proportion
The slides are examples picked because the liquidity was taken and price then moved. They do not say how often that happens. When you backtest, count three things for each marked level: taken and reversed, taken and continued, and never reached.
